slides: So, before you practice, let's go over the whole number line in a few minutes.
Every rule, every trap. Short, and quick.
It all starts with four ranges.
Below minus one, negative fractions, positive fractions, and above one. Every number in a range behaves the same way.
Watch the borders. And if they only say x is positive... well, it could be below one, or above one.
The negative side is a mirror. So look at the positive side, and then mirror the picture.
So what do multiplying and dividing do? One is the dividing line.
Now, that's for positive numbers. A negative number makes the same moves... away from zero, or toward zero.
And times a NEGATIVE number? You jump to the other side of zero, and the order flips.
Hierarchy. A number in a higher range stays bigger, after any positive power or root.
Seven sixths is above one, and three quarters is a fraction. So don't calculate the roots.
For negative numbers, it's odd powers and odd roots only.
The same operation on two positive numbers? Ignore it. And weak times weak loses to strong times strong.
Exceptional powers move a number into another range. So handle them first.
An even power of a negative number turns positive. But read the brackets. Without them, minus four squared is minus sixteen.
A negative exponent? To compare ranges, flip it first. Here a fraction became a number above one.
The arrows show what a bigger power does in each range.
Right means bigger, left means smaller. And on the negative side, odd powers only.
A positive fraction: a bigger power gives a smaller number. And the root goes the other way.
So, three steps. Exceptions, roots into powers, and then the arrows. With the arrows, you can keep a negative exponent.
And if they give the order and ask for the range? Use the arrows backwards... or plug in.
The reciprocal, one over x, keeps the sign. Big and small swap.
A quarter becomes four. Four becomes a quarter. And the negative side is the mirror.
For numbers with the same sign, the reciprocal flips the order.
Not sure? Plug in. One number from each allowed range.
A root in the choices? Pick a number with a clean root.
And change only the unknown. If you change the numbers in the question, you can change the answer.
Read the question word. Necessarily, or could?
To find a counter-example, push the values to the edges of their ranges.
A picture of the line? Write the range under each letter. It's not drawn to scale, so trust the order, not the distances.
And last, distance and midpoint.
The midpoint is the average. A third of the way? Take a third of the distance, and walk it from the start.
So, before you practice, always ask yourself:
The common traps: ignoring an operation on negative numbers, forgetting that a positive x can be a fraction, and trusting the distances in a picture.
Well... you know all of this. Go practice.
